The Federal Open Market Committee, or FOMC, is the part of the Fed that makes key decisions about several things, including the federal funds rate. The [most recent meeting](https://www.forbes.com/sites/tylerroush/2026/06/17/fed-holds-interest-rates-unchanged-in-kevin-warshs-first-meeting-but-higher-rates-are-expected/) was in June. The FOMC’s officials typically submits their individual projections of gross domestic product (GDP) growth, the unemployment rate and inflation for the current year, as well as for the following two and then for the “longer run.” The inflation figures used are the Personal Consumption Expenditures produced by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, which is the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation. For each year, 2026 through 2028, and then the longer run, the dots show how the Fed executives projected the midpoint of the federal funds rate range for each year. It is in the FOMC meetings that the Fed can change a basic interest rate that affects many others, which has implications for corporate earnings.
